title: Help Jeehye fight aggressive uterine sarcoma
story:
Jeehye has built her life around helping other people. As an instructor with the nonprofit Marshmallow Minds, her dream job is bringing math, science and STEAM classes to children in under-resourced schools across San Jose. She is the person who steps forward when someone else needs care. Now she is the one who needs a community to step forward for her.

In early June, excruciating abdominal pain sent Jeehye to an emergency room in the United States. Doctors believed a degenerating uterine fibroid was causing the pain and said it needed to be removed. She traveled to Korea for the operation, expecting surgery to close a frightening chapter.

The procedure was successful, but the pathology results changed everything. Doctors found an abnormality in the tissue and called her back on July 23. The following day, a specialist confirmed the diagnosis her family feared: Jeehye has uterine sarcoma, an aggressive cancer.

What was supposed to be recovery from a fibroid operation became the beginning of a cancer fight in a matter of days. Jeehye is undergoing further testing to determine the stage and the safest treatment plan. Her medical team is strongly recommending surgery and chemotherapy.

IMAGE:fh/jeehye-2.jpg|

Jeehye does not have health insurance in Korea. Hospital fees and follow-up chemotherapy are expected to cost tens of thousands of dollars, and treatment also means she cannot return to the work and children she loves. Every week away brings medical expenses and basic living costs with no regular income to absorb them.

Her fiancé, Alex, and her parents are doing everything they can. But love cannot pay a hospital bill, and this family should not have to calculate how much cancer treatment they can afford while waiting to learn how far the disease has progressed.

The $58,000 goal is an estimate based on the expected treatment journey and will be updated as doctors confirm the plan. Donations will help pay for testing, surgery, chemotherapy and Jeehye's living expenses while she is unable to work. It is not simply financial relief—it is time, access to care and the chance to keep fighting without treatment being delayed by money.

IMAGE:fh/jeehye-3.jpg|

Jeehye has spent her career opening doors for children who had fewer opportunities. Today, we can open a door for her. Please donate now if you can, and share her story with someone who may help. Aggressive cancer does not wait for a family to feel ready, and Jeehye should not have to face it alone.

— Alex Lee, Jeehye's fiancé

title: Help Julie Fight Cancer
story:
Juliet is 6 years old who has been diagnosed with stage 2 chronic leukemia.

A time for princess dresses, learning to ride a bicycle, and losing her first tooth. Instead, Juliet is learning about chemo cycles, hospital wards, and the brutal reality of leukemia, an aggressive childhood cancer.

IMAGE:fh/juliet-2.jpg|

Her treatments are expensive and overwhelming, but we’re not giving up.

Every share, or donation helps us more than you can imagine.

IMAGE:fh/juliet-3.jpg|

Thank you for standing with us during the hardest moments of our lives. God bless you

title: Lilah, 3, danced through brain cancer — now she's fighting for every child who can't
story:
On February 24, 2025, Katelynn gave birth to her son William. It should have been the happiest day of their lives. Instead, it became the day their daughter Lilah's body suddenly went stiff, her eyes rolled back, and she stopped responding.

In the same hospital where a new baby was being welcomed, doctors were telling Lilah's parents something no parent can survive hearing: there was a mass in her brain. It was large. It was aggressive. And it was already stealing her.

The diagnosis was ATRT — atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor. A name most people cannot pronounce. A cancer so rare and so brutal that when a family hears it, they are usually told to prepare for the worst. Most children do not survive it. The ones who do survive because strangers before them funded the research that built the treatment.

Lilah was one year old when surgeons cut open her skull to remove the tumor. Then came five rounds of chemotherapy so toxic it destroys adult bodies. High-dose chemo with stem-cell rescue. Six weeks of proton radiation. Infections. Fevers. Nights when her parents didn't know if she would see morning.

And through all of it, Lilah danced.

IMAGE:fh/lilah-1.jpg|

In a hospital gown with tubes attached to her tiny body, she danced for the nurses. She danced in the hallway. She walked into appointments clutching a slice of pizza, smiling like she owned the room. Sweet. Silly. Fiercely mighty. That is who she is.

In mid-December, her family got the words they had prayed for: no evidence of disease. Her spine MRI was clear. Lilah had beaten a monster that kills most children it touches.

But here is the truth that keeps her mother awake at night: ATRT comes back. It comes back for too many children. And when it does, there is almost nothing left to try. The only way to change that ending is research — and research needs money.

Every 2 minutes, somewhere in the world, another child is diagnosed with cancer. Somewhere tonight, a mother is being told her baby has a mass in their brain. That family will stand in the same hallway Lilah's family stood in. They will cry the same tears. They will beg the same God. And whether their child lives or dies will depend, in part, on whether people like us decided to fund the science that saves them.

Lilah's life was saved by research paid for by people who never knew her name. Now her family is asking you to pay it forward — for the next Lilah. For the child who is being diagnosed right now while you read this.

"I pray every night," her mother says, "let me see the beautiful woman I know she will become. And let her save someone else too."

🎗️ Please donate. $20. $50. $100. Whatever your heart allows. Every dollar funds childhood cancer research — the trials, the labs, the science that turns a death sentence into a second chance. If you cannot give, share this page. One share can reach the person who saves a child's life.

title: Help Me Continue My Fight for Life – Stage 4 Metastatic Cancer
story:
In 2025, my life changed forever when I was diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer. I began chemotherapy, but after one session I had a severe reaction that nearly took my life and I was unable to continue safely. Soon after, another metastatic diagnosis changed everything again and our world was turned upside down.

I went from walking independently to needing a wheelchair and crutches. It has been an overwhelming and heartbreaking journey for me and my family.

Because chemotherapy is not a safe option for me, I have spent the past seven months pursuing alternative treatment, including hyperbaric oxygen therapy, organic nutrition, and essential vitamins and minerals. We have seen encouraging signs of improvement and I deeply want to continue.

IMAGE:fh/nalize-2.jpg|

Unfortunately, these treatments are not covered by insurance. I am unable to work, and our household income has dropped from two incomes to one, making it impossible to sustain ongoing costs.

Funds raised will go directly toward my continued treatment, including oxygen therapy sessions, organic food, supplements, and a healing retreat.

IMAGE:fh/nalize-3.jpg|

I am not ready to give up. I have 3 boys, the youngest is 17 & my husband who all are holding onto hope with me. We are doing everything we can to fight for more time together.

Any support, no matter how small, would mean more than words can express. Thank you for standing with us on this journey. Your kindness and support gives us hope to keep fighting for life each day, and to keep believing in healing.

title: Help Mia Fight Leukemia
story:
My name is Rachel, and I'm writing this from a hallway in the pediatric oncology wing where my daughter Mia is finishing her third round of chemotherapy. If you had told me six months ago that I'd be asking strangers for help, I wouldn't have believed you. But here we are — and I'm so grateful you're reading this.

Mia is eight. She loves painting, her rescue puppy Coco, and telling jokes she doesn't quite get yet. In March, after weeks of unexplained bruising and fatigue, we got the diagnosis no parent wants to hear: acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Since then, our lives have been reorganized around a treatment plan that stretches over the next 24 months.

Insurance covers the treatment itself, but it doesn't cover the reality of what this year looks like for our family. The specialty hospital is 4 hours from home. My husband and I have taken unpaid leave in shifts. Our older son is staying with grandparents. The bills that fall between the cracks — lodging, gas, meals, co-pays, the endless small things — are what this campaign is for.

IMAGE:fh/unsplash-1576091160399-112ba8d25d1d-1200x800.jpg|

Here's exactly where the funds go: about $18,000 covers lodging near the hospital for the remaining inpatient stays. Roughly $12,000 covers travel and lost wages for the parent who needs to be there at every appointment. Around $15,000 covers medical co-pays that aren't waived. The remaining $5,000 is a buffer for the emergencies that keep finding us.

If you've made it this far, thank you. Truly. Every single donation — $5 or $500 — is a small vote of confidence that our family is going to be okay. And on the hard days, that matters more than I can explain.

IMAGE:fh/unsplash-1559757148-5c350d0d3c56-1200x800.jpg|

— Rachel, Mia's mom

title: Help my children survive in Gaza
story:
My name is Wafaa. I am a mother in Gaza, and I am writing this with my phone at 3% battery, sitting on the floor beside my children while the sky shakes above us.

Last night my little girl pressed her face into my shoulder and said, "Mama, my stomach hurts." I checked her for fever. I looked for a wound. There was nothing to find. The pain was hunger. There was no food left to give her. I held her and I cried in the dark so she would not see my face.

That is what this war has done to us. My children no longer ask for toys. They ask for bread. They ask if the bombing will stop before morning. They wake up screaming and hide in corners of a room that has no windows left in it.

I have three children who urgently need medication and medical care. The hospitals near us are destroyed or so overwhelmed that a child with an infection waits behind a hundred people with shrapnel wounds. Medicine that used to cost almost nothing is now impossible to find at any price.

IMAGE:fh/gaza-child-sitting.png|

My brother was hit during the war and lost his hand. He was the one who used to carry water for all of us. Now he needs treatment and a prosthetic limb just to live with dignity again — around $50,000 that our family will never have on its own.

Food is scarce. Clean water is rationed by the litre. We boil what we can find. We eat once a day, and on the worst days the children eat and the adults do not.

We are trying to evacuate 19 adults and 9 children from Gaza before it is too late. The crossing costs are brutal: about $12,500 for each man, $8,500 for each woman, $3,000 for each child. Every day we wait, another name on that list may not need a ticket anymore.

I am not asking for comfort. I am asking for survival. $20 is flour, rice and clean water for my children this week. $50 is the medication one of them needs and cannot get. $100 is a step closer to carrying a child across the border to safety. $250 helps move one more child out of the range of the bombs.

IMAGE:fh/gaza-child-crying.png|

If you cannot give, please share. A share costs you nothing and it is how strangers found us in the first place. Someone reading this because of you may be the reason my children see next month.

I do not know how to end a message like this except with the truth: my children are alive right now. While you read this, they are breathing, and they are hungry, and they are scared. Please do not scroll past them.

From the bottom of our hearts — thank you for standing with us when hope feels so far away. 🤍🇵🇸

title: Help Namulisa live with eye cancer
story:
Hi, my name is Maddy and I am fundraising to help Namulisa live with the medical condition she has. At only 13 years old, her world is slowly fading into a blur of shadows. Instead of chasing butterflies in the fields near her village, she wakes up every morning to sharp, stabbing pain radiating through her head.

The diagnosis is retinoblastoma — eye cancer. What started as a strange white glow in her pupil, first noticed by her grandmother under the dim light of a kerosene lamp, has become a protruding mass that has stolen her sight and her smile.

Her family, already struggling to put food on the table, is heartbroken. Her grandmother has sold their only two goats to pay for the initial consultations, but the cost of the life-saving chemotherapy and surgery needed to stop the cancer from reaching her brain is a mountain they cannot climb alone.

"I just want to go back to school," Namulisa whispers, her hand instinctively covering her bandaged face. "I don't want the dark to take the rest of me."

Namulisa urgently needs financial assistance for medical bills, transport to the city hospital, personal needs, and specialized care. Your kindness could be the light that guides her out of the darkness. Thank you.

title: Help Nicole fight cancer as a single mother
story:
My name is Nicole. I am a single mother, and I am fighting cancer alone.

I never wanted to be the person asking strangers for help. I worked. I paid my bills. I was the one who showed up for everyone else. Then the diagnosis came, and everything I had built started falling apart in weeks.

There is no second parent in this house. No second income. When I am in the infusion chair, nobody is earning. When I am too weak to stand, my kids are the ones bringing me water and pretending they are not scared.

Chemotherapy takes everything. The nausea, the exhaustion, the days I cannot get off the bathroom floor. And on top of that: co-pays, prescriptions, the rides to the cancer center, the rent that does not pause because I am sick.

IMAGE:fh/nicole-avatar.jpg|

Last month I had to choose between a prescription and groceries. I bought the groceries, because my children eat first. Skipping medication is how a treatable cancer becomes a terminal one — and I know that, and I still had to make that choice.

I am not asking for a comfortable life. I am asking for time with my children. Time to see them grow up. Time to be their mother instead of a patient they visit.

Here is exactly what your help does: $20 buys the anti-nausea medication that lets me keep food down. $50 covers a co-pay or a ride to the cancer center. $100 fills the fridge for a week when I cannot work. $250 keeps the lights on and the rent current so my kids are not moved out of their home in the middle of treatment.

IMAGE:fh/nicole-cover.png|

If you cannot give, please share. Every share reaches someone who can, and that is how I have made it this far at all.

To everyone who has already helped: you have no idea what it means to be a mother who was drowning and felt someone reach for her hand. Thank you. Please don't stop now. 🙏

— Nicole

title: Noah is fighting for his life — without the bill paid, treatment stops
story:
Noah is not old enough to say his own name. He is old enough to be intubated, sedated, wired to a ventilator, with a feeding tube taped across his face and cancer moving through a body the size of your forearm.

There is a photo of him screaming on an examination table, arms flung out, before anyone could explain to him what was about to happen. There is another of him awake in intensive care, eyes open, exhausted, looking at his mother as if to ask when this ends. Those pictures are the whole reason this page exists.

Noah is fighting desperately for his life. And the brutal truth his family has to say out loud is this: without the bill paid, there is no treatment. Not delayed treatment. No treatment. In the middle of a child's cancer fight, the machine stops when the money stops.

His mother has not gone home. She sleeps beside him, learns the alarms, holds the small hand between the tubes, and begs the nurses for one more good hour. She has spent everything she had — savings, wages, help from family — and it is gone. Every cent of it went into him.

IMAGE:fh/noah-2.jpg|

What is left is the part she cannot pay: the hospital bill standing between Noah and his next round of treatment. That is what your donation buys. Not paperwork. Not overheads. His chemotherapy, his intensive care days, his medication, his oxygen and feeding supplies.

$20 covers a dose of his medication. $50 pays for a day of the care keeping him alive. $100 covers supplies for his intensive care bed. $250 pays down the bill that decides whether his treatment continues this week.

If you cannot give, share him. Every single donor on this page arrived because someone refused to scroll past a baby on a ventilator.

IMAGE:fh/noah-3.jpg|

Noah is still fighting. He has not given up. Please do not let a bill be the thing that takes him.

— Noah's family

title: Help Samuel fight AMC — a single father asking for help
story:
My name is Daniela. I'm Samuel's aunt, and I'm writing this for my brother Daniel — Samuel's dad and his only parent. He works day and night for this boy, so I'm the one asking for help on his behalf.

Samuel was born with Arthrogryposis Multiplex Congenita (AMC) — a condition that stiffens and locks his joints and keeps his muscles from developing the way they should. From his very first day, his little body has had to fight for every movement other children make without thinking.

His mother left when the diagnosis got hard. Since then it's been just the two of us. I work every hour I can, and every dollar goes to Samuel — his specialist appointments, his physical therapy, his braces and splints, the helmet that protects his head, the adapted equipment he needs just to sit, sleep and grow safely.

IMAGE:fh/samuel-1.jpg|

I am not ashamed to say it: I cannot do this alone anymore. AMC doesn't pause. Every month without therapy, Samuel's joints stiffen a little more, and some of that loss is permanent. The doctors are clear — consistent treatment now is the difference between a boy who learns to move, stand and one day walk with support, and a boy whose body closes in on him while we wait.

We are raising $5,000 to cover Samuel's essential treatment: weekly physical therapy sessions, orthopedic follow-ups, new splints and braces as he grows, and the transport to get him to every single appointment. Nothing extra. Nothing wasted. Every dollar goes directly to his care.

If you've ever watched someone you love struggle and felt helpless, you know what my days feel like. Samuel smiles through all of it — through the pain, the exercises, the long drives. He doesn't know we're behind on bills. He just knows his dad is there. I want to keep being able to say that.

🙏 Every donation, no matter how small, brings us closer to the treatment Samuel needs this month. If you cannot donate, please share this fundraiser — it could reach someone who can change this little boy's future.

💙 Please stand with Samuel. And if you can, stand with a father who refuses to give up on his son.

title: Help Stephanie, 29, fight breast cancer for her son
story:
Hi, I'm Stephanie. I'm 29 years old — a mom to a beautiful little boy, a wife, and a proud third-grade special education teacher. For the past year, I have been battling breast cancer.

My diagnosis came while my husband and I were trying for baby number two and trying to buy our first home. In one moment, both dreams suddenly felt impossible.

Thanks to the generosity of so many people, I was able to pay for fertility preservation before treatment, 20 rounds of chemotherapy, surgery, and six months without an income — because teachers don't get paid when they're out on medical leave.

But cancer doesn't stop the bills. Life in New York City is expensive, and while it's where the best doctors for my care are, it's also where my whole life is. When I learned I would need radiation and another 15 rounds of treatment, the financial weight became overwhelming, and I was forced to go back to work before I was truly ready.

IMAGE:fh/stephanie-2.jpg|

This disease has taken so much from me. It took my income. It took precious time with the people I love, including the chance to fully be there when I lost a family member. It took relationships I thought would survive anything. It put my dream of giving my son a sibling on hold, and delayed the dream of giving him a home of our own.

As a mom, all I can focus on now is giving him a childhood. A childhood where there is always food on the table. Where Mommy still gets down on the floor to play with him. Where he knows he is deeply loved — and doesn't have to carry the weight of knowing how sick his mom is.

Your support helps cover weekly chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radiation and medications; hospital bills; fertility preservation costs; unpaid leave and lost summer income; childcare during treatment and recovery days; tolls, gas and parking for weekly trips into the city; a medically necessary diet; my husband's lost income while caring for me; and the debt and household bills that kept coming all year.

If you can help — through a donation, by sharing this page, or with a simple prayer — it means more to our family than words can express. Every act of kindness lifts a weight off our shoulders and lets me focus on healing and being present for my son.

Thank you for reading my story. Please remind the women in your life to check themselves — early detection saves lives, and it might just save mine. Most of all, thank you for helping me give my son a childhood filled with love, stability and hope, even in the hardest season of our lives.

With love, Stephanie

title: Help support Isla's journey through leukaemia
story:
Our dear friends Gena and Riley have just received the most devastating news a parent could ever imagine — their beautiful 2-year-old daughter Isla has been diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

In an instant, their world has been turned upside down. Isla has already begun intensive treatment, and the road ahead will be long and incredibly tough.

IMAGE:fh/gfm-92186769_1751024018368813_r.jpg|

Gena and Riley are also parents to 5-year-old Flynn, and Gena is currently 35 weeks pregnant, with baby number three due in just a few weeks. In the middle of this unimaginable storm, they are doing everything they can to hold their little family together.

We are hoping to raise enough to cover Riley's income — so he can step away from work and be fully present with Isla during her treatment, and support Gena as she prepares to give birth. Your donations will go directly toward medical expenses, everyday bills, and caring for Flynn and their soon-to-arrive newborn.

IMAGE:fh/gfm-92186769_1751024293245126_r.jpg|

This is a family who would never ask for help — but they desperately need it right now. Any amount, big or small, will make a real difference. And if you can't give, please share this with your community. Every show of support counts.

title: Hope for Baby Axel's journey
story:
As a parent, nothing is more difficult than watching a child face a serious illness. Every day brings new challenges — hospital visits, medical tests, treatments, and uncertainty. What should be a time filled with laughter, milestones, and happy memories has instead become a journey of courage, strength, and hope.

Axel is currently receiving ongoing medical care and requires continued treatment, medications, specialist appointments, and regular monitoring. The emotional and financial strain of providing this care has become overwhelming, but giving up is not an option.

Every contribution, no matter the size, goes directly toward making sure Axel receives the care he needs.

The support of family, friends, kind strangers, and the wider community means more than words can express. Whether through a donation or simply sharing this fundraiser, every act of kindness brings hope and helps lighten the burden during an incredibly difficult time.

Thank you for taking the time to read Axel's story and for being part of this journey. Your generosity and support make a real difference and provide hope for brighter days ahead.

title: Surgery for Idris — congenital heart disease (TGA)
story:
Hi, my name is Sara Almeida and I'm here asking for help for my 1-year-old son Idris. Idris was born with severe congenital heart disease — Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA).

This means his heart formed with the main arteries switched, causing blood to circulate the wrong way. Doctors said he needs urgent surgery. Every day without treatment is a serious risk to his life.

IMAGE:fh/gfm-104059739_1782328768619606.jpg|

We're seeking specialized treatment abroad, because this type of surgery isn't available to us here. Funds raised will go toward the cardiac surgery, hospitalization, medications, exams, travel, and treatment.

Every amount helps: $20 helps with medications, $100 helps with exams, $500 brings us closer to surgery. A single share can reach someone who can save Idris. From the heart, thank you.

title: Itamar rehabilitation support
story:

story:

The photograph on this page is difficult to look at. Katrina lies surrounded by medical equipment, her small face almost hidden by the care her body needs. For Maria, this is not an image she can close. It is the reality beside her every day.

Alessia Tasca created this fundraiser as a messenger and caretaker for Maria. She is helping a young mother say the words she never wanted to need: I cannot save my daughter alone. Please help me.

Every donation helps carry the cost of Katrina's treatment and the aftercare she will need. A small gift joined with another can become the support that keeps her journey moving forward. Sharing her story can put it in front of the person able to make that next gift.

Maria is not asking anyone to fix everything alone. She is asking thousands of people to refuse to leave a five-year-old child and her mother alone in the hardest fight of their lives.

Please donate if you can, and share Katrina's story if you cannot. Give this little girl the chance to grow beyond hospital rooms, treatment days and leukaemia.

— Maria, Katrina's mother, with Alessia Tasca

title: Nepal floods: emergency relief for families and children
story:
On the morning of August 26, a wall of water came down the mountain without warning. A large section of glacier broke away on the Nepal–Tibet border and sent a torrent through the valleys below. In minutes, homes, roads and bridges were gone. Whole villages simply are not there anymore.

Nepal Police have confirmed 389 people dead and 466 injured. More than 1,300 people are still missing — including over 700 foreign nationals from two dozen countries. 28 police officers who went in to rescue people are among the missing. Search teams are still digging.

A CNN crew that reached one of the devastated zones described what is left in three words: "It is uninhabitable."

The roads used to reach the worst-hit districts — Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading — have been destroyed. Helicopters are the only way in, and teams on foot are pushing through thick mud and debris to reach people who have been waiting days with nothing. The UN has released US$2 million for water, medical kits and emergency shelter, and has said plainly: it is not close to enough.

IMAGE:fh/nepal-2.jpg|

And it is not over. Three more days of rain are forecast. Landslide debris is piling up into unstable natural dams. Chinese authorities have issued a high-risk warning about a lake on the border that could burst and flood the same valleys again. An earthquake was recorded in Tibet the same week. The people who survived Wednesday could lose everything a second time.

The children are paying for this the hardest. Kids who lost their parents in the water are now sitting in camps with no clean water, no dry clothes, no blankets, and no one left to look for them. Some of them have not eaten a full meal since the flood came through.

We have combined two emergency appeals into one so every dollar moves faster: medical response for flood survivors, and direct aid for the affected children of Nepal. This fund pays for exactly what is missing on the ground right now — clean water, food, blankets, tents, wound care, antibiotics and essential medicines carried in by mobile medical teams working in the districts helicopters can barely reach.

IMAGE:fh/nepal-kids-1.jpg|

This is not a someday emergency. Every hour that passes, another survivor with an open wound gets an infection that did not need to happen. Another child spends another freezing night outside. Another family gets hit by the next landslide because nobody got them out in time.

Please give today. If you cannot give, share this — the families in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading do not have a voice loud enough to reach you on their own. 🙏

title: Nicolas is 2 years old — his liver cancer has spread to his lungs
story:
Nicolas Trujillo is two years old. He should be filling a house with noise right now — running from room to room, dropping toys, refusing to nap. Instead he is recovering from cancer surgery, and his family is staring at bills they have no way of paying.

Nicolas was diagnosed with cancer of the liver. Then came the sentence no parent survives hearing calmly: it has spread to his lungs. Two organs. One two-year-old body. A fight most adults would not be able to carry.

On the 7th of August he went into surgery. His parents handed their baby to strangers in scrubs and waited in a corridor with nothing to hold on to but each other. He came through it. He is still here. He is still fighting.

But surviving surgery is not the end of this — it is the beginning of the expensive part. Scans to see whether the lungs are responding. Follow-up appointments. Medication. Specialist visits. Each one arrives with a price attached, and each one is not optional if Nicolas is going to live.

IMAGE:fh/nicolas-2.jpg|

His family is already struggling to pay for all of his medical bills. They are not asking for comfort or convenience. They are asking for the difference between treatment that continues and treatment that stops because an invoice went unpaid.

This is Nicolas: the son of my mother's best friend, a little boy I have watched grow, now with an IV line taped to an arm too small for it. He does not understand what cancer is. He understands that it hurts, and that his mum is there.

Every dollar donated here goes into his care — his surgery costs, his scans, his medication, and the hospital bills already sitting on the kitchen table.

$20 covers a dose of his medication. $50 pays for a hospital day. $100 helps cover a scan of his lungs. $250 clears a bill his parents cannot clear alone.

If you cannot give, please share his page. Most people who donate to Nicolas got here because someone refused to scroll past a two-year-old with cancer in two organs.

Please help us give this little boy the chance to grow up. God bless, and thank you.

— John Bourn, organiser

title: Help Chika Beat Cancer – Surgery No.4 & Restart Immunotherapy
story:
In December 2024, I was diagnosed with a rare type of kidney cancer called Eosinophilic Cystic and Solid Renal Cell Carcinoma (ECS RCC), barely 3 years after I also lost my mum to cancer.

With no cure or standard method of treatment for this cancer, I’ve survived 4 rounds of surgery, lost my right kidney and some of my left kidney, and in June 2026, a mass was found in my jaw that had to be surgically removed.

After my second surgery in January 2026, I struggled with paralysis, urinary incontinence, loss of hearing in my right ear, drastic vision loss, and loss of kidney function.

IMAGE:fh/chika-2.jpg|

In March 2026, my doctor recommended immunotherapy, which has since proved to be a great decision for my health. However, the cost of fighting a rare cancer in the United States has been a huge factor. Over $500k in medical debt, and I truly cannot continue this way. A single bag of infusion for immunotherapy costs $80,000. A single bag!

After much consideration, I decided to explore treatment in Asia, and after multiple rejections from hospitals overseas due to the rare nature of my cancer and fear that my hospital in the US is trying to dump me on them, two hospitals have decided to accept my case and continue treatment. While the cost is a lot less, I still do not have the means to go across the world for the medical care I need.

IMAGE:fh/chika-3.jpg|

Please, I need your help. I refuse to give up on myself. I have so much life in me. I fight a good fight, and I am a worthy opponent!

Please help a girl get her life back and beat cancer

title: 40 orphans in Uganda are out of food — Redeemer's Hope is their only family
story:
There are children in this world who have no one. No mother. No father. No one coming. In Uganda, dozens of them end up at the same small door: Redeemer's Hope Orphanage.

These children lost their parents to disease, poverty and tragedy — and now they are struggling with the most basic needs a human being can have: clean water, one real meal a day, clothes without holes, a roof that doesn't leak when it rains, a classroom to sit in, and medicine when fever comes at night.

The team at Redeemer's Hope has given everything they have. They stretch every shilling until it breaks. They skip their own meals so the children eat. But love doesn't pay for rice, and faith doesn't buy antibiotics. They cannot do this alone anymore — and the children's needs don't wait for a better month.

When a child at the orphanage gets sick, there is no insurance card. There is no emergency fund. There is a volunteer holding a feverish child and praying someone, somewhere, decides to care. Tonight, that someone could be you.

Every dollar raised here goes directly to the orphanage: food for the month ahead, clean water, school fees so these kids aren't condemned to repeat the poverty that orphaned them, clothing, bedding, and the essential healthcare that stands between a treatable infection and a funeral no child should ever need.

For these children, hope isn't a feeling — it's a plate of food, a safe bed, a school uniform. Things you can literally buy for them today.

🙏 Please donate whatever you can. $20 feeds a child. $100 stocks the medicine shelf. And if you cannot give, share this page — one share can reach the person who changes forty lives at once.

title: Save a life — help us save our little girl
story:
There is a little girl lying in a hospital cot right now with a feeding tube taped to her cheek and oxygen tubing across her face. She is too weak to sit up. She is too tired to open her eyes for long. And she is far too young to understand why the people who love her keep crying in the corridor.

This is what cancer looks like when it happens to a child. It is not a poster. It is not a statistic. It is a bed rail, a monitor beeping through the night, a mother whispering "please stay with me" while the machines answer instead.

Her family has done everything a family can do. They have sat through every appointment, learned words no parent should have to learn, held her hand through needles and scans and nights that never seemed to end. They have already given every dollar they had. There is nothing left to give except this plea.

The treatment has not stopped yet — but it will if the money runs out. That is the terrible arithmetic this family wakes up to every morning: her next dose, her next scan, her next admission all have a price, and they cannot pay it alone.

IMAGE:fh/savelife-1.jpg|

So they are asking strangers. They are asking you. Not because they want pity, but because a child's life should never depend on how much her parents earn.

Every gift on this page goes straight into keeping her treatment running: hospital fees, medication, oxygen and feeding supplies, and the transport that gets her to the ward when she is too fragile to wait. Nothing here is abstract. A donation today becomes care tonight.

$10 is a dose. $25 is a set of supplies. $50 keeps her on the ward. $250 pays down a bill that is currently standing between her and her next treatment.

IMAGE:fh/savelife-2.jpg|

If you cannot give, share this page. Most of the people who saved a life this year did it because a friend refused to scroll past. Please be that friend today.

She is still here. She is still fighting. Please do not let her fight it alone.

— KAWUMA EDRINE FERLAND, organiser

title: Standing with Nurse Nyki in Her Cancer Battle
story:
Hi, my name is Nyki.

I’m 24 years old. I’m a nurse. I’ve spent my career caring for others, holding hands during hard diagnoses, comforting families, and advocating for my patients.

I never imagined I would become the patient.

In 2024, I was diagnosed with an aggressive form of colon cancer. Since then, I’ve undergone major abdominal surgery, including an ileostomy to preserve my intestines, and I am currently receiving chemotherapy.

As a nurse, I know what these words mean. I understand the scans. I understand the labs. I understand the statistics. But nothing prepares you for hearing them about yourself.

IMAGE:fh/nyki-2.jpg|

I am a full time mom to my 3 year old son, Jamari. He doesn’t understand cancer. He just knows Mommy gets tired. He knows Mommy has a bag on her stomach now. He knows Mommy goes to the hospital a lot.

Chemo has made it impossible for me to work right now due to cancer pains. The same hands that once cared for others are now too weak some days to care for myself. Losing my ability to work has been one of the hardest parts of this journey. I have always been independent. I have always provided.

Now I’m learning how to receive.

This fundraiser will help with medical expenses not covered by insurance, transportation to treatments, basic living expenses while I’m unable to work, childcare support on treatment days, and everyday stability so I can focus on healing.

Cancer is heavy. Being a young mom with cancer is heavier.

IMAGE:fh/nyki-3.jpg|

But I am fighting. I am showing up. I am believing that God still has a purpose for me beyond this diagnosis.

If you feel led to donate, share, or pray, I am deeply grateful. Every act of kindness helps me keep going not just for me, but for my son.

Thank you for standing with the nurse who is now learning what it means to be cared for.

With love, Nyki

title: 27 new tumors — help Brittany keep fighting cancer
story:
Brittany Christianson has already been through more than most people could imagine. She went through radiation to treat a large tumor in her back, holding on to the hope that the worst was behind her.

Then the latest scans came back. They showed 27 new tumors, on top of the one she had already fought so hard to treat. Our family is still trying to understand what this means for the road ahead.

Because there are so many tumors, her doctors say they first need to bring them under control before they can even attempt surgery or more radiation. We are exploring clinical trials and waiting for a definitive plan. Waiting is its own kind of pain when every day matters.

Anyone who knows Brittany knows she is a fighter. Her spirit is unmatched, and she has faced every step of this with a courage that leaves us speechless. But her body needs rest now — it is carrying more than any body should.

IMAGE:fh/brittany-2.jpg|

That means Brittany cannot work during this time. Her income has stopped, but the bills have not. Appointments, scans, medications, travel and everyday living costs keep coming, and they are mounting faster than our family can keep up.

We never wanted to ask for help. But we would rather ask than watch Brittany spend her strength worrying about money instead of fighting for her life.

Your donation helps cover her medical and living expenses so she can focus on one thing only: getting through the treatment ahead.

IMAGE:fh/brittany-3.jpg|

If you can't give, please share her story or send a prayer her way. Every bit of love truly helps, and Brittany feels every single one.

We appreciate you more than words can say. Thank you for standing with Brittany. ❤️

title: Support Jayvion’s Fight Against Leukemia
story:
On August 10th, our lives changed completely when my 12-year-old son, Jayvion, was diagnosed with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). What started as a frightening health concern quickly became a diagnosis no parent ever wants to hear.

He is now in the hospital receiving treatment and chemotherapy, and we know we will be here for quite some time. How long his hospital stay will be depends on his upcoming test results and how his body responds to treatment, but there is a possibility that we could be facing a much longer journey than we initially expected.

Right now, my entire focus is being by my son’s side, advocating for him, comforting him, and helping him through one of the hardest battles of his life. At the same time, I have my daughter at home who still needs me, and I have to make sure she is cared for and supported while I am spending so much time at the hospital. I am also trying to take care of myself enough to be strong for both of my children.

IMAGE:fh/jayvion-2.jpg|

This has brought unexpected financial challenges with hospital stays, food, travel, household bills, and everyday expenses continuing while our lives are centered around Jayvion’s treatment.

I never imagined I would have to ask for help like this, but right now, we truly need our community. Any donation, no matter the amount, would mean more to us than I can put into words. If you aren’t able to donate, sharing our story, sending prayers, and keeping Jayvion in your thoughts would mean just as much.

IMAGE:fh/jayvion-3.jpg|

We are taking this one day at a time and praying for good test results, successful treatment, and most importantly, for my son to come home healthy.

Thank you for standing with Jayvion and our family during this incredibly difficult time

title: Support Luna's journey to recovery — help her beat cancer
story:
Luna should be learning new words right now. Instead she is learning the sound of an IV pump, the sting of a needle, the smell of a hospital corridor at 3am. She is a baby. She is a cancer warrior. And she is waiting for a surgery her family cannot afford.

Her mother has barely left her side. She sleeps in a chair beside the cot, holds Luna against her chest when the fear gets too big for such a small body, and whispers the same promise over and over: I am right here. Just a mom fighting beside her baby.

Luna's condition is serious and her surgery is urgent. This operation is not optional and it is not something that can wait for a better month — it is critical for her health and for the future she still has every right to have.

The family has already given everything they had. Appointments, scans, medication, the drives to the hospital, the days of work lost sitting in waiting rooms — it has drained them. The cost of the surgery ahead is far more than they can manage on their own. That is the only reason this page exists.

IMAGE:fh/luna-2.jpg|

Every donation goes straight into Luna's care: her operation, her hospital bills, and the recovery that follows once the surgery is finally behind her. Nothing abstract. Nothing wasted. Just a little girl getting the treatment she deserves.

$20 covers her medication. $50 pays for a hospital day. $100 helps cover the tests her surgeons need first. $250 moves her surgery from 'someday' to a date on the calendar.

If you cannot give, please share her page. Almost every donor here arrived because someone refused to scroll past a baby fighting cancer.

IMAGE:fh/luna-3.jpg|

Luna is still fighting. Her mother is still fighting. Please help them win this.

— Davon Jackson, organiser

title: Support Melissa's fight against cancer
story:
Hi, my name is Melissa. I'm 30 years old, and I have cancer.

Just a few weeks ago, my life changed in a way I never could have imagined. On the way home from my dress rehearsal dinner for my wedding, I was involved in a serious car accident where I was T-boned. I was taken to the emergency room, and during imaging, doctors discovered multiple masses throughout my body — on my chest, near my heart, and in my abdomen.

The ER doctors told us they strongly suspected lymphoma and that further testing was urgently needed. Now they believe I could have undifferentiated spindle cell sarcoma, or possibly both lymphoma and sarcoma. Neither of my biopsies has given definitive results yet.

Within hours, Matt and I had to walk into our own wedding carrying devastating news and so much uncertainty. Shortly after, I began seeing specialists at Vanderbilt and underwent two biopsies — and they are currently stumped.

IMAGE:fh/melissa-2.jpg|

Looking back, I had been experiencing pain and other symptoms for some time, but I believed they were related to my autoimmune disease. Over the past few weeks my condition has worsened. Simple daily tasks have become painful, and walking has become difficult. I am now preparing to begin chemotherapy and have to have a second biopsy due to other complications.

In addition to everything else, the car accident created another major financial hardship. My car was totaled, and insurance did not cover the full amount owed on the vehicle. I am now left owing money on a car I no longer have — an unexpected expense during an already overwhelming time.

The financial burden has become significant. I am currently unable to work, and while Matt continues working, adding me to his insurance has increased our monthly expenses by nearly $1,000. Between everyday bills, medical expenses related to chemotherapy and treatment, insurance costs, and the remaining balance on my totaled car, we are struggling to stay afloat.

IMAGE:fh/melissa-3.jpg|

I know my focus right now needs to be on healing, resting, and fighting this disease — not worrying about how we will make ends meet. Asking for help does not come easily to me, but we truly need support during this season.

Any donation, share, or kind word helps more than I can express. Your support will go directly toward medical expenses, insurance costs, transportation needs, and basic living expenses while I undergo treatment. Thank you for being part of our village and for helping us get through this incredibly difficult time.

With love and gratitude, Melissa

story:
# Help Jaterria Survive Her Health Battles and Rebuild Her Future

**At just 24 years old, Jaterria has already endured more medical emergencies and heartbreak than anyone should have to face in a lifetime. And now, she needs our help.**

Her life changed after a devastating stroke left her struggling to do things most of us take for granted.

She had to relearn basic movements, including how to crawl and turn over.

**Imagine having to fight to regain control of your own body, only to lose your mother to cancer while you're still recovering.**

That is what Jaterria experienced.

But her suffering didn't end there.

Over the following years, she was placed on life support three times. She suffered a second stroke in August 2026. Then, on October 11, 2026, she experienced a heart attack.

IMAGE:uploads/campaigns/jaterria/jaterria-4.webp|Jaterria during her recovery

Today, Jaterria continues to face heart failure, pulmonary complications, and significant vision loss.

**And now, at only 24, she is preparing for her second heart surgery.**

Despite everything, Jaterria has refused to abandon her dreams.

She earned her associate degree in computer science, obtained her barbering license, and continues working toward her bachelor's degree in computer engineering technology.

**Jaterria has already fought through two strokes, a heart attack, and the loss of her mother. She shouldn't have to face the financial burden of recovery alone.**

title: Help Jeremiah Fight Stage 4 Bone Cancer
story:
# Help 19-Year-Old Jeremiah Fight Stage 4 Bone Cancer

**At just 19 years old, Jeremiah is fighting a devastating battle against Stage 4 bone cancer. And his family needs your help.**

While most teenagers are making plans for college, their careers, and the future, Jeremiah has spent some of the most important years of his life facing surgeries, chemotherapy, radiation, and the painful uncertainty of cancer.

It all began during his senior year of high school.

What started as severe back pain and difficulty walking turned into a diagnosis that changed everything.

**Doctors discovered an extremely rare and aggressive cancer that had spread from his spine to his chest, jaw, and hip.**

Jeremiah underwent multiple spinal surgeries and exhausting rounds of treatment.

IMAGE:uploads/campaigns/jeremiah/jeremiah-3.webp|Jeremiah in the hospital

Then came another devastating moment.

**After surgery, Jeremiah became paralyzed.**

He was told his chances of walking again were very small.

Imagine being a teenager and suddenly having to fight to regain something as simple as taking a step.

But Jeremiah refused to give up.

Through countless hours of rehabilitation, determination, and hope, he began learning to walk again.

Even while battling cancer, he achieved something extraordinary: **he graduated from high school in June 2024.**

His courage is remarkable. But his medical journey is far from over.

IMAGE:uploads/campaigns/jeremiah/jeremiah-4.webp|Jeremiah during his recovery

### Then came another heartbreaking setback.

In February 2025, after 14 cycles of chemotherapy, Jeremiah learned that his cancer had returned and continued to spread.

His doctors have explained that he will need ongoing treatment, potentially for the rest of his life.

More chemotherapy. More radiation. More rehabilitation. And possibly more surgeries.

**No 19-year-old should have to carry so much pain and uncertainty while trying to build a future.**

And as Jeremiah continues his treatment, his family faces another enormous challenge: the financial burden.

The cost of medical care, ongoing treatment, rehabilitation, and everyday expenses continues to grow.

**His family wants to focus on helping him through this difficult journey, but they cannot carry the financial weight alone.**

### This is where your kindness can make a difference.

Whether you give $20, $50, $100, or any amount you can afford, your compassion can make a meaningful difference.

**Jeremiah has already fought through cancer, paralysis, multiple surgeries, and a devastating relapse.**

He is still working toward recovery. Still holding on to his dreams. Still trying to build a life beyond hospital walls.

**Please, help Jeremiah continue receiving the care and support he needs.**

Every donation matters. And because his treatment needs are ongoing, even a small recurring contribution can provide valuable support.

If you cannot donate, please share his story.
